final_letter: unreadable (if forced, ז over ו; not ס)
shape_evidence: The glyph is short and sits on the baseline at about x-height. It has a heavy blob at top right, narrows in the middle, and widens into a wedge-shaped foot at bottom left.
It has no closed round bowl, so it is not ס. The samekh in איינגעסאַלטעט on the same line is a clearly closed round letter, and this glyph looks nothing like it.
It is not a plain vertical stroke. The crops show a real leftward foot and an S-like tilt from upper right to lower left.
comparison_evidence: Vavs in ווירד (same line, same typeface): straight, even-width vertical strokes with only a slight head and no foot. The uncertain glyph is wider, pinched in the middle, and has a foot, so it does not match these vavs well.

Zayin in החרוזים (scan16): a heavy head on top of a fairly straight stem, with no clear leftward foot. The uncertain glyph's heavy head fits a zayin better than a vav, but its leftward foot is not in the scan16 zayin. Scan16 may also be a different typeface or size, so it is only weak evidence.

Gimel in the same word (פֿאָלגענדע, 4th letter): has a leftward foot at the base, which is the closest shape match among nearby letters. But the gimel is taller with a straighter stem, and ג is not one of the candidates being judged here. I'm noting the resemblance only as shape evidence, not proposing it as the reading.
The blur and ink spread in the scan could make a zayin's head and the end of its stem look like this shape, or could hide a damaged or different letter.
unresolved: ז vs ו: the shape leans toward ז (heavy head, wider body) more than ו, but the leftward foot is not in either clear exemplar.
The foot looks like the gimel in the same word, so there may be a damaged or atypical letter here that is none of ז/ו/ס.
A higher-resolution scan, or another example of zayin from the same Yiddish typeface (scan 57, not scan16), would be needed to settle it.
I did not use the likely German word (Folgendes) to choose the letter. ס is ruled out by its shape alone.
